newsitem.title: USA: Maine voters seen voting on Gov.'s timber proposal.
newsitem.headline: Maine voters seen voting on Gov.'s timber proposal.

text.p: Maine's voters likely will get to choose or reject different plans that would limit the paper industry's ability to cut wide swaths of trees, as the Senate on Friday seemed set to put the governor's plan on the ballot.
Maine's legislature on Thursday began a special session called by Gov. Angus King, who wanted them to approve a less radical plan to limit clear-cutting than one submitted by the Green Party.
King's proposal would restrict clear-cutting to a 75-acre swath instead of the current 250-acre limit; the Green Party would totally ban this method of harvesting trees.
If both proposals make it to the November ballot, Maine voters will be able to choose whether to approve one of them or reject them both.

The House attached four amendments to the bill proposed by the governor before sending it on to the Senate, but a spokesman for King on Friday said they probably would not cause the governor to reject the bill.

"They're some that we probably can live with, no dealbreakers," said Dennis Bailey, a spokesman for King, though he added the governor would like the Senate to delete an amendment adding six new forestry jobs.

He explained that King was concerned about the costs of the new jobs. Another amendment, which would give the legislature the right to appoint four of the seven members of a forestry oversight board, was criticized by Bailey but he does not see it causing the governor to turn the bill down.

The special legislative session also is considering a technical measure that would allow Maine to accept block welfare grants. Without the bill, the state could lose $9 million to $12 million due to the sweeping changes in the federal welfare program, which relies heavily on block grants for the states.

Another bill would give the C.F. Hathaway Co factory, which is owned by Warnaco Group and located in Waterville, tax incentives in an effort to make the sale more attractive for a group of new investors.
The unprofitable factory, which makes shirts, employs around 450 workers.
And a fourth bill covers how tips are handled by restaurant workers.
